sentences.text: Muraenosaurus was named for its eel-like appearance, characterized by a long neck and small head. Nearly half of its length was its neck, which possessed up to 44 vertebrae. Its head was notably small compared to the total size of the animal, measuring only 37 centimeters in length.
The largest known specimen of Muraenosaurus measured up to 5.2 meters in length, though other sources suggest it could grow up to 6 meters.
Muraenosaurus possessed 66 pre-sacral vertebrae, 44 of which were cervical, bringing the total number of vertebrae in its body to 79.
The coracoids of Muraenosaurus reached widths of nearly 14 inches. The forelimbs of Muraenosaurus were compressed mediolaterally compared to its hind limbs and those of other plesiosaurs.

The original Muraenosaurus specimen may have been damaged due to the casual collection style of Charles Leeds. The first recovered Muraenosaurus specimen was missing pieces of the skull and many caudal vertebrae.
Muraenosaurus leedsii is the most complete and only undisputed species within the genus Muraenosaurus.
The first specimen of Muraenosaurus was collected by Charles E. Leeds and described by H. G. Seeley. The genus Muraenosaurus was first described by British paleontologist Harry Govier Seeley in 1874.
Muraenosaurus likely preyed on teleost fish and cephalopods. Its teeth were long, thin, and slightly curved backward, reinforcing the belief that its main diet consisted of fish and cephalopods.

Researchers propose that Muraenosaurus may have fed on benthic fish by floating above them and reaching down with its head. Muraenosaurus may have used a benthic grazing strategy to harvest immobile species like cephalopods from the sea floor.

Gastroliths are frequently found in plesiosauromorph stomachs and are associated with this body type. Models indicate that swallowed stones may have reduced pivoting at depth and dampened neck oscillations, helping provide stability against underwater currents.
Muraenosaurus was likely preyed upon by apex predators such as pliosaurs and crocodylomorphs like Liopleurodon and Pliosaurus.
Its tail was relatively small and primarily served a stabilizing function during swimming. Its trunk was compact and rigid, a characteristic that favored efficient movement in water.
Muraenosaurus belongs to the family Cryptoclididae. Muraenosaurus belongs to the subfamily Muraenosaurinae.

H. G. Seeley initially classified Muraenosaurus in the family Elasmosauridae rather than Cryptoclididae. The similarity between Muraenosaurus and elasmosaurs is now understood as a case of convergent evolution.

Although some researchers previously related it to elasmosaurs due to its long neck, modern phylogenetic analyses show it shares a closer relationship with genera like Cryptoclidus and Tricleidus. These evolutionary relationships were established through comparative study of skull characteristics, cervical vertebrae, and limbs.

Muraenosaurus lived between 160 and 164 million years ago during the Callovian stage of the Middle Jurassic. The time range for Muraenosaurus is from the Callovian to the Oxfordian, between 165.3 and 154.8 million years ago.

Muraenosaurus lived in the shallow, warm Oxford Clay sea, which had an average depth of less than 50 meters. Fossils were discovered in the Oxford Clay Formation in England, a Middle Jurassic geological formation rich in marine reptiles.
Fossils of Muraenosaurus have been found in the Oxford Clay deposits of southern England and parts of France.
It is debated whether Picrocleidus beloclis should be considered synonymous with Muraenosaurus due to doubts about their relationship.
It was initially debated that long-necked plesiosaurs were strictly fish-eaters based on their conical teeth.
